events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.
Theo proposes Theo, Amara. As leader on Mission 1 with no role information, I'm including myself as a Loyal Servant to show good faith and pairing with Amara to spread trust across the table.

I appreciate Theo including me on this team — it's a reasonable opening proposal with just two spots on Mission 1. As a Loyal Servant with no private information, I'm comfortable going on this mission. That said, I'd like to keep a close eye on Noah going forward — something about their approach hasn't sat well with me. We should be watchful as we move into later missions.

I'll speak plainly since Amara put my name on the table: I don't know what 'approach' she's referring to, because I haven't taken one. I'm a Loyal Servant with no private information, same as most of us, and the only thing I've done so far is sit quietly while the leader made a sensible opening proposal. If watching me makes her feel useful, fine — but I'd ask everyone to weigh whether that suspicion is based on anything concrete or just a vibe. Vibes on Mission 1 are how Good burns votes on nothing.

On the team itself: Theo and Amara is a fine pairing. Two players, no information anywhere at the table, so there's nothing to second-guess. I have no objection to it and I'd rather see Mission 1 pass cleanly than churn through rejections before anyone has learned anything. A fail here tells us one of two people is evil, which is a genuinely useful data point, but I'd still prefer trust to start us off.

I'll just note for the record that I'm comfortable either way this vote goes — approving it or rejecting it costs us little at this stage. What I won't do is manufacture suspicion out of thin air, which is more than I can say for some early observations floating around this table.

The proposal itself is standard for Mission 1, but Amara's comment regarding Noah immediately caught my attention. Prior to your statement, Noah had not said or done anything aside from sitting at the table, so what specific 'approach' were you picking up on, Amara? Fabricating reads before anyone has acted can distract town from real data, so I'd appreciate you clarifying what actually prompted that suspicion.

Lucia's challenge is fair, and I owe the table more than a vibe. What prompted my comment on Noah was their demeanor before and during Theo's proposal — a stillness and composure that struck me as slightly rehearsed rather than natural. On Mission 1 with no information, that's admittedly thin, and I won't pretend it's more than an instinct. But instincts are all any of us have right now, so I'd rather voice mine early than sit on them.

Noah, I'll say this directly: your response was well-constructed — almost too smooth for someone caught off guard. That could be nothing; maybe you're just a calm player. But the combination of that composure and the pointed way you pushed back at me is what stuck with me. I'm keeping you on my watchlist, not convicting you.

On the team: Theo and Amara remains a perfectly fine Mission 1 proposal. I'm comfortable being on it, and I think we should get this mission underway rather than burn rejections on a two-person team with no red flags.

Leo, now that you've heard both sides of this Noah exchange — does my read have any merit to you, or do you think I'm chasing shadows here?

Amara, I’ve heard both sides. Your read on Noah is too thin to act on: composure isn’t a mission card. Noah’s reply was defensive but coherent, and I don’t see concrete evidence. That doesn’t mean your instinct is worthless, only that it shouldn’t drive a vote on Mission 1. The proposal itself is standard: Theo and Amara on a two-person team with no role information available. I’d rather see a clean vote and an actual mission result than reject a reasonable opening team over a vibe. I’m inclined to approve. If it fails, we learn something; if it succeeds, we’ve started cleanly.

Leo, I appreciate you weighing in, but you're being too quick to wave off the concern. You say my read on Noah is 'too thin to act on' — yet you also concede Noah's reply was 'defensive.' Defensive is exactly what I flagged. The concern was never just that Noah was composed; it's that Noah went from silent to a full-throated, well-structured defense the moment a name was mentioned. That's a lot of work for someone who claims they've done nothing.

Look at what Noah actually did: preemptively framed all suspicion as 'vibes on Mission 1,' claimed comfort either way to project trustworthiness, and closed by subtly redirecting blame. Every element of that response was designed to shut down inquiry before it started. You read that as reassuring; I read it as someone who knows how to manage a table.

What concerns me is the pattern: Noah deflects, and within one turn Leo arrives with a measured, reasonable-sounding defense saying the suspicion is 'too thin.' I'm not convicting anyone — but when an accused player and their defender push the identical line (trust the team, don't overthink it), I pay attention.

On the proposal itself: failThreshold is 1 on this mission. One fail card kills Mission 1. The two seats on this team are therefore critical. I trust Theo's leadership and I'm confident in my own alignment, but this is not a mission where we should rubber-stamp anything.

Leo, you said Noah's reply was 'defensive but coherent.' Beyond its overall tone, was there any specific line in Noah's message you found genuinely reassuring — or did you simply find the polish convincing? I'd like to know what substance you're actually reading into it.

Amara, you asked what specific line in Noah’s message I found reassuring. Honestly, none — it was the overall calm, not a particular sentence. But that is exactly why your escalation concerns me. A thin Mission 1 instinct is one thing; turning it into a ‘pattern’ involving me because I gave a measured response is another. You are asking the table to treat polish as proof and disagreement as coordination. I don’t buy that, and I don’t want to approve a two-person team with a failThreshold of 1 when one member is pushing a case this hard on this little. I’m now leaning reject unless you can offer something concrete beyond tone and the fact that Noah defended himself. Lucia, you challenged Amara earlier about her initial read — does her latest turn give you more confidence in her or less?

Leo, to answer your question directly: Amara’s latest turn gives me considerably less confidence in her. She began by targeting Noah over unprompted 'demeanor,' criticized him for defending himself coherently, and then immediately framed your measured assessment as a coordinated 'pattern' between the two of you. Treating a calm defense as guilt and treating rational disagreement as conspiracy is either reckless town play or evil actively manufacturing division. On Mission 1 with a failThreshold of 1, approving Amara after watching her escalate unsubstantiated accusations across the table feels like an unnecessary gamble, and I am currently leaning reject. Theo, as the leader who selected Amara, how do you view her escalation against Noah and Leo, and are you planning to maintain this team or revise it before we vote?

Lucia, thank you for asking directly. I selected Amara on a two-player team with no information on Mission 1, so I didn't pick her for any reason beyond spreading trust. Her escalation against Noah and Leo has gone further than the evidence supports. Noah's reply was measured, and Leo's answer was a reasonable reading of it, not a coordinated defense. Calling that a pattern is a stretch, and I'd like Amara to explain what concrete action from Noah or Leo justifies it. I'm not convinced she's Evil based on this alone, and I'm not convinced Noah is either. I'm keeping the team as proposed for now. I'm on it myself, and with one fail card ending Mission 1, I would rather we vote on the merits than revise to a new partner based on tone. If the table moves toward rejecting, I'll consider a different second member, but I'm not planning to change it right now.

I came into this discussion prepared to approve a standard Mission 1 team, but Amara’s latest turn moved me firmly toward reject. The issue is not that she had an early instinct about Noah; early instincts are normal. The issue is that when challenged, she escalated a thin read into a claimed pattern involving both Noah and me, treating a calm defense and a measured disagreement as evidence of coordination. That is not concrete mission evidence, and with failThreshold 1, the second seat on this team matters too much to wave through that kind of escalation. Theo has handled the proposal reasonably and I am not accusing him; my concern is specifically Amara’s willingness to manufacture a broader case from tone and pushback. If Amara had offered one specific action from Noah or me that justified the pattern, I would reconsider. She has not. On a one-fail mission, I would rather reject this team than reward that reasoning, and I encourage the table to do the same.

Leo and Lucia have made their objections clear, and I take the table's concerns seriously. I still have no information that Amara is Evil, and I don't think her early read on Noah alone justifies rejecting Mission 1. But Leo's point that her escalation rested on tone rather than action is fair, and with one fail card ending this mission, I don't want to push a team the table doesn't trust. Amara, before the vote, please name one concrete action from Noah or Leo that supports the pattern you described, or acknowledge that the pattern was an overreach. I'm holding the team for now and will revise the second seat only if the objections stay this strong after your answer.

Final statement from me before the poll. I'm holding Theo and Amara as proposed for now. I'm on the team myself, so I have a direct stake in it passing only if it's sound. Amara has not yet answered the request in my last message for one concrete action from Noah or Leo that supports her pattern claim. Until she does, the table's objections are reasonable, and I'll revise the second seat if they remain this strong after her answer. If nobody has a new concrete point, I'd ask the table to vote on the team's merits rather than on tone. My own vote will be an approve on this team, and I'll accept the table's decision on it.

I'll keep this brief and focused on the actual decision in front of us. Amara has now spent three turns building a case against me, and none of it contains a single concrete action — only tone, composure, and the fact that I answered her when she named me. At this point I'm not going to keep litigating my own demeanor. I said my piece, Leo and Lucia have both independently found her escalation unconvincing, and Theo himself acknowledged the objection rests on nothing actionable. What matters now is the seat, not the argument.

On a Mission 1 with failThreshold of 1, the second seat on this team belongs to someone the table has lost confidence in — and that's not about whether Amara is Evil, it's about whether five players can vote approve on a team containing a member they've spent an entire discussion distrusting. The answer is clearly no. I support Theo revising the second seat and moving on. I'd rather that happen now than burn a rejection on a team everyone already agrees is compromised by doubt.

I'll add one thing for the record: I'm not asking anyone to apologize or walk anything back. Instincts get voiced on Mission 1, that's fine. But the standard Amara applied — treating a calm response as suspicious and a measured disagreement as coordination — is a standard that will fracture every future discussion if we accept it. This table should reject that reasoning now, while the cost is one rejection instead of a wasted mission.

Lucia, one direct question since you raised the revision path with Theo: if the second seat is swapped, do you have a preference for who replaces Amara, or do you want Theo to choose freely?

To answer your question directly, Noah: I want Theo to have the discretion to choose, but if he decides to revise the second seat, I would gladly step onto the team myself, or see him select either you or Leo. What matters most is restoring consensus to that second seat.

Amara has exhausted all three of her speaking turns without offering any concrete action to back up her claims of a coordinated pattern. Treating composure as guilt and normal table pushback as conspiracy is toxic logic for town, and on a mission with a failThreshold of 1, placing someone who operates like that onto the team is an unacceptable risk.

Theo, since Amara has not answered your condition and has no turns remaining to do so, the objections stand firm. If you submit Theo and Amara to a vote, I will vote to reject it. If you use your leader revision to replace Amara, I am prepared to approve and let Mission 1 proceed cleanly.

Lucia, thank you for the direct answer — Theo choosing freely, with you, me, or Leo as acceptable replacements, is exactly the kind of flexibility that gets Mission 1 done without another round of conflict. Since Amara is out of turns and never produced a single concrete action to back her pattern claim, I think the path forward is clear: the table should reject Theo and Amara as proposed, and Theo should immediately revise the second seat.

On who should take that seat: I'll make the case for Leo. He engaged with Amara's argument on its merits, asked her for specifics, and only moved toward reject when she escalated from a thin instinct into an accusation of coordination against him personally. That is exactly the kind of level-headed, evidence-first reasoning you want on a two-person team where a single fail card decides the mission. Lucia already named him as acceptable, and I agree — he's earned the trust of this table through how he's handled being dragged into a baseless narrative. I'd be comfortable with that team and would vote approve.

For transparency about myself: given that Amara spent three turns painting me as suspicious without evidence, I think it would be a mistake for Theo to pick me. Not because there's anything to it, but because a mission decided by one fail card shouldn't carry even manufactured doubt. A clean team of Theo and Leo lets us get a real result and move on.

To be clear on the vote itself: I'll reject Theo and Amara as currently constituted, and support Theo and Leo if Theo makes that revision.

Theo revises the team to Theo, Lucia. Amara did not answer the request for a concrete action, and Lucia, Leo, and Noah all objected to her. I'm replacing the second seat with Lucia, who challenged Amara's read early and has been consistent. I'm on the team with her.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Lucia proposes Lucia, Theo, Leo. Mission 1 succeeded cleanly with Theo and myself. Leo demonstrated sound, objective reasoning throughout Mission 1's discussion and approved the winning team, whereas Noah unexpectedly rejected it and Amara pushed unsubstantiated division.

Lucia, I appreciate you including Theo from Mission 1, but I have strong objections to Leo in the third seat. Look at how Leo operated in Mission 1: he rushed to defend Noah the moment I raised a concern, then within two turns flipped entirely to voting against the team. That is not consistent reasoning — that is someone reading the room and adjusting position based on what keeps them safe. Leo went from "your instinct is too thin to act on, I'm inclined to approve" to "I'm now leaning reject" without any new evidence between those statements. The only thing that changed was the social pressure, and Leo followed it precisely.

I stand by what I said in Mission 1: Noah's response was too polished for someone caught off guard, and Leo's defense of him arrived suspiciously fast. I was removed from the team for that position, and I accept that. But now Leo is being rewarded with a team seat after playing both sides — defending Noah publicly while ultimately voting the same way as everyone else. On a three-player team where one fail card ends Mission 2, I don't trust someone whose reasoning shifted purely to match the table.

Theo, you handled Mission 1 well by adjusting to the table's concerns. I'd ask you to apply that same judgment now: do you actually trust Leo's independent reasoning, or did he just give you two well-measured statements that happened to align with wherever the room was heading?

Amara’s objection to me rests on a mischaracterization. In Mission 1 I did not “rush to defend Noah”; I said his reply was defensive but coherent and that her initial read was too thin to act on. What changed my position was her later turn, where she escalated a thin instinct into a claimed pattern involving both Noah and me because I gave a measured response. That was new content, and it was reasonable to treat it as a risk on a mission where one fail card decides the outcome. When Theo revised the team to remove that risk and include Lucia, I approved the revised team. That is not “following social pressure”; it is responding to what was actually said.

On the current team: Lucia, Theo, and Leo. Mission 1 succeeded with Theo and Lucia. Lucia has been consistent, challenged weak reasoning early, and made a proposal that keeps the successful core together. I am on the team myself, and I support it. Amara’s current objection does not identify a concrete action by me that was suspicious; it re-labels my reaction to her own escalation as opportunism. That is still tone and narrative, not evidence. I will vote to approve this team.

Lucia, I understand keeping the successful core from Mission 1, but I need to flag serious concerns about Leo in the third seat — this is exactly the seat I'd be most worried about with one fail card deciding Mission 2.

Look at Leo's Mission 1 trajectory: he opened by saying he was inclined to approve, then flipped to reject mid-discussion without any new concrete action from anyone. His own stated reason was that Amara escalated — but his vote shift conveniently aligned with where the table was heading. He didn't lead that shift; he followed it. Now he's being rewarded with a team seat for it.

More importantly, on a three-person team with failThreshold 1, Leo occupies a critical seat. If Leo is Evil, one card from his hand ends Mission 2. I'm not saying he is — I'm saying he hasn't earned the kind of trust that justifies handing him a mission-critical seat over Noah, who at least directly stated he'd support a revised team and gave clear reasoning.

Theo, you handled Mission 1 by adjusting when the table raised legitimate concerns. I'd ask you the same question now: what has Leo actually done to deserve this seat more than the alternatives? His Mission 1 reasoning was sound but reactive — he changed position based on social dynamics, not evidence. Is that the profile you want on a mission where one fail card is decisive?

Amara, you asked directly, so here is my answer. Yes, I trust Leo's reasoning on this team. In Mission 1 his position moved for a specific reason: he said your first read on Noah was too thin to act on, and when you escalated it into a claimed pattern involving him personally, he identified that as new content and moved to reject. That is a response to a concrete point, not a shift to match the table. He also asked you for a concrete action by Noah or Leo, which is what I asked of you too, and you did not provide one. I also don't accept that he 'rushed to defend Noah'; his first statement was that Noah's reply was defensive but coherent. Leo then approved the revised Mission 1 team, which succeeded. I'm on this team myself, so I have a direct stake in it being sound, and I will approve it. If you have a concrete action by Leo, not a change in tone, name it and I will weigh it.

I've made my case twice and I'll make it once more, then the table can decide. My concern with Leo is not about tone — it's about the pattern of his positions tracking social convenience rather than evidence. In Mission 1, he opened inclined to approve, then reversed to reject once the room shifted. Now he's on a team being rewarded for exactly that alignment. On a three-player mission with one fail card, I need confidence that every seat is earned through independent reasoning, not through agreeing with whoever spoke last.

Theo, you asked me to name a concrete action by Leo. Here it is: in Mission 1, Leo stated he was inclined to approve, then said he was leaning reject — and by his own admission, nothing concrete changed between those two statements except that I escalated. He reacted to social pressure, not to new evidence. That is a concrete behavioral observation, not a vibe.

Here is my constructive ask: Mission 1 succeeded with Theo and Lucia. Those two seats are proven. For the third seat, I'd ask the table to consider me. I was removed from Mission 1's team because I voiced an instinct the table found too aggressive — and that instinct was never disproven, just voted aside. I've been consistent in my concerns, I have no record of shifting to match the room, and I'd bring exactly the kind of firm, independent reasoning you want on a mission where one fail card is decisive.

Theo, you said you'd weigh a concrete action if I named one. I've named one. Given that, would you at least consider replacing Leo with me before we vote, or is your position that social reactivity is acceptable on a one-fail mission?

Amara, my answer is no, I won't replace Leo with you. You asked whether social reactivity is acceptable on a one-fail mission. It isn't, but that isn't what happened with Leo. His Mission 1 position changed after you escalated a thin read into a claimed pattern that named him personally. He said at the time that this was new content, and changing a vote in response to a specific accusation is what a careful player does. Your claim that he followed the room rests mainly on the fact that he ended up where the table was, which is true of nearly every vote.

I also don't think rerunning Mission 1's discussion helps. The team I first proposed with you on it was rejected, and when asked for one concrete action from Noah or Leo, the closest thing you gave was Leo changing his vote in reaction to your escalation. Mission 1 then succeeded with the revised team of Theo and Lucia. I'm not treating that as proof that anyone is Good, but it is the only hard data we have so far.

I'm keeping this team and I will approve it. Lucia's proposal keeps the seat that succeeded on Mission 1 and adds Leo, who has engaged with the arguments on their merits and has not made a claim about anyone's alignment without a stated reason. If you have a specific action by Leo that is different from a change in his stated position, name it and I'll weigh it. Otherwise I'd ask the table to vote on this team's merits.

I'll keep this short since the substance hasn't changed since the last time I addressed one of Amara's cases. Her objection to Leo is the same structure she used on me in Mission 1: a shift in position reframed as a character flaw, and a disagreement with her treated as evidence of something sinister. Theo has already laid out exactly why Leo's Mission 1 move was a response to new content — Amara's escalation into a claimed pattern that named Leo personally — and Amara's counter was to cite that same vote change as her one 'concrete action.' A player changing their stated position in response to a specific accusation directed at them is not evidence of anything except that they were paying attention.

I'll note one thing about my own Mission 1 reject vote for the record, since it's the only wrinkle anyone could raise against my consistency: I voted reject on the revised team because I had argued for Leo to take the second seat and Theo chose Lucia instead. That was a preference, not an accusation, and the mission succeeding with Theo and Lucia settles it — I was wrong to let a seating preference cost a vote, and I said at the time the team itself was fine.

On the current proposal: Lucia, Theo, and Leo is a sound Mission 2 team. Theo and Lucia are proven together on a clean Mission 1, and Leo has been the most consistently evidence-driven voice at this table across both discussions. Amara's argument again asks us to treat reasoning patterns as mission risk on a one-fail mission, and I'd repeat what I said in Mission 1: that standard fractures every future discussion if we accept it, because any player who ever changes their mind becomes suspect.

I support this team and will vote to approve it.

I proposed this team based on the clean success of Mission 1 with Theo and myself, paired with Leo's sound, objective evaluation of the board throughout both rounds of discussion. Amara has now spent another three turns trying to undermine that logic, attempting to reframe Leo's rational pushback against her unprompted escalation as opportunism. As Theo rightly pointed out, adjusting one's stance in response to a direct, unsubstantiated accusation is careful play, not social reactivity. Amara's push to replace Leo after offering zero concrete evidence—repeating the exact same playbook from Mission 1—only solidifies my lack of confidence in her. With Theo, Leo, Noah, and myself all aligned on the merits of this roster, we have clear consensus. I am keeping the team as Lucia, Theo, and Leo, and I am ready to move to the vote.

The board has not changed since my last statement, and I don't think it needs to. Lucia, Theo, and Leo is a sound Mission 2 team, and I support it. Theo and Lucia are the only proven combination we have — they delivered a clean Mission 1 with zero fail cards. Leo has been the most consistently evidence-driven player across both discussions: he asked Amara for specifics in Mission 1, gave a measured assessment, and only adjusted his position when she escalated a thin instinct into a claimed coordination pattern that named him personally. That is careful play, not opportunism.

Amara has now exhausted all three of her speaking turns, and across all of them she offered exactly one 'concrete action' against Leo: that he changed his stated position after she publicly accused him of coordinating with her target. Read that again — her sole evidence is that Leo responded to being accused. By that standard, any player who ever defends themselves or updates on a direct accusation becomes suspect, and every future discussion becomes an exercise in punishing people for reacting to the table. I said this in Mission 1 and I'll say it once more: that standard is poison, and it is also a playbook. Amara has now run the identical structure twice — thin behavioral read, escalation under challenge, reframing measured pushback as conspiracy. Twice is a pattern, and this time it is not a pattern she gets to project onto others.

I'd also point out the practical math. It's Mission 2, we have one success on the board, and this team of three carries two players from that success plus the player Amara has spent six turns trying to discredit without a single concrete action. Rejecting this team wouldn't remove any risk — it would just hand influence over the third seat to the one player at this table who has demonstrated a willingness to build cases from tone. That is the opposite of what Good should want on a mission where one fail card decides the outcome.

Nothing new is coming. Amara is out of turns, Theo and Lucia have both stated they're keeping the team, and Leo has answered the objection directly. The only remaining value in this discussion is putting the question to the table. I encourage everyone to vote on what's actually in front of us: a team with two proven seats and a third seat held by the most consistently reasonable player here. I'm voting approve, and I'd like to see this mission decided by mission cards rather than another round of manufactured doubt.

This is my last speaking turn, so I'll keep it short. I'm on this team, and I'm approving Lucia, Theo, and Leo. Theo and Lucia already delivered a clean Mission 1, and that success is the only hard data we have. On Leo, my earlier view stands: his Mission 1 vote moved after Amara escalated a thin read into a pattern that named him, and he asked for a concrete action before he decided. Amara has asked for a change in this seat without offering a new action by Leo, so I don't think the seat should change. I have no role information, so I'm relying on the board. Everyone has now stated their position, so I'd ask the table to vote on this team's merits.

I support the proposed team of Lucia, Theo, and Leo. Lucia and Theo are the only pair with a clean Mission 1 result, and I have already explained my Mission 1 position: I moved against Amara’s original team only after she escalated a thin read into a claimed pattern naming me personally, and I approved the revised team that succeeded. Amara has now used all three Mission 2 turns to repeat the same objection without identifying any new concrete action by me. Her sole example remains that I changed my stated position after she accused me of coordination — which is a response to her accusation, not independent evidence against me. On a one-fail mission, I understand scrutiny of every seat, but rejecting a team built on the only proven pairing and replacing it with the player who has twice run the same unsupported escalation would not reduce risk. I will vote to approve Lucia, Theo, and Leo.

Lucia confirms Lucia, Theo, Leo. The table reached strong consensus around keeping the successful core of Theo and myself while adding Leo, whose reasoning has been sound and evidence-based. Amara has offered no actionable evidence against him, so I am maintaining the proposed team of Lucia, Theo, and Leo.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 2 fails (1 fail cards).

Amara proposes Amara, Theo. Mission 3 requires 2 players. I know Leo and Noah are Evil — Leo was almost certainly the fail card on Mission 2's team, and Noah has been shielding him all game while Amara's instincts pointed their way. Theo is the safest Good seat: he succeeded cleanly on Mission 1, handled leadership responsibly, and has no association with the failed Mission 2 trio. This team excludes both players I believe are Evil with no mission involvement from either.

Amara’s proposal rests on a claim the table cannot verify: she says she knows Leo and Noah are Evil. That is not a read — it is an assertion of private knowledge. If she is Good without a role that gives her that, she cannot know it. If she does have such a role, she is painting a target and still has not explained why Theo is the safest Good seat when Theo was also on the failed Mission 2 team. The only public data is that Mission 2 failed with one fail card among Lucia, Theo, and Leo. Amara treats Leo as almost certainly the fail and Theo as clean, but she was not on that mission and cannot know which of the three submitted it. Her proposal conveniently excludes both players she accused, includes herself, and gives a pass to another member of the failed team. After two missions of building cases from tone and then escalating to claimed certainty, this is not evidence-first play; it is narrative control. On a one-fail Mission 3, I will not approve a team whose leader asks us to accept unverifiable knowledge and selective exoneration. I am voting reject and I would ask the table to reject until we get a proposal grounded in public results rather than Amara’s declared certainty.

Amara’s proposal asks the table to accept that she knows Leo and Noah are Evil. That is not public evidence; it is a private-knowledge claim, and it cannot be verified from the board. More troubling, she treats Theo as the safest Good seat even though Theo was on the failed Mission 2 team with Lucia and Leo. Publicly, one fail card came from that trio, and Amara has offered no public basis for exonerating Theo while declaring me guilty. Her team excludes the two players she names and includes herself plus a member of the failed team — selective certainty. On a one-fail Mission 3, I will reject a team built on unverifiable claims and selective exoneration. If Amara has a concrete public reason for treating Theo as clean and me as Evil, she should state it. Otherwise the table should reject and require a proposal grounded in mission results rather than declared certainty.

Amara’s proposal asks the table to accept a private-knowledge claim — that she knows Leo and Noah are Evil — while the only public evidence is Mission 2 failing with one fail card among Lucia, Theo, and Leo. She declares Leo almost certainly the fail and Theo the safest Good seat, but she was not on that mission and cannot publicly distinguish which of the three submitted the fail. That is selective exoneration, not evidence-first reasoning. Her team also includes herself with no mission result supporting her and excludes both players she has accused, which conveniently removes scrutiny from her own seat. After two missions of thin behavioral reads escalating into claimed certainty, this proposal repeats the same pattern at a point where one fail card decides Mission 3. I will vote reject, and I encourage the table to reject until we get a team grounded in public mission results rather than Amara’s declared certainty and selective trust.

Amara's proposal asks this table to accept something no Mission 3 discussion should be built on: a declared certainty that cannot be checked against anything public. She says she 'knows' Leo and Noah are Evil. Either that is a private-information claim she needs to justify, or it is a lucky guess dressed up as knowledge. If she has a role that gives her that information, she should say so plainly instead of using it as a bludgeon to hand-pick her own team. If she does not, then what she is really doing is asking us to exclude two players and exonerate one member of the failed Mission 2 team on her word alone.

And that exoneration is the part that should trouble everyone most. The only hard data on the board is that Mission 2 failed with exactly one fail card among Lucia, Theo, and Leo. Amara was not on that mission. She cannot know who submitted it. Yet her proposal declares Leo 'almost certainly' the fail while calling Theo the safest Good seat at the table. Why? What did Theo do between Mission 2 and now that clears him in her eyes? Nothing she has said answers that. Selecting which member of the failed team is clean and which is guilty, with no stated basis, is not evidence — it is exactly the selective certainty she has been accused of before.

I want to be clear about my own position, since Amara has now publicly named me Evil twice. I have no way to prove what I am, and I won't waste the table's time asking for trust on my word alone. What I will point to is my record: I argued for Leo in Mission 1, voted reject on the revised team over a seating preference, and have consistently demanded concrete actions over tone-based reads. Amara, by contrast, has now run the same escalation in three straight discussions, and each time her target list has grown while her evidence has stayed at zero.

On the team itself: Amara and Theo includes one member of the failed Mission 2 trio and one player whose case rests entirely on unverifiable certainty. With failThreshold at 1 on this mission, that combination deserves real scrutiny, not a rubber stamp based on who Amara has decided to exclude. If the table wants a Mission 3 team grounded in actual results, it should start from the fact that the fail card came from Lucia, Theo, or Leo — and treat all three with equal suspicion until something distinguishes them.

rules:
1. Players and teams

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

Mission team sizes for missions 1–5:

| Players | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 |
| 6 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 4 |
| 7 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 4 |
| 8 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 9 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 10 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
